title: Questioning Your Own Sources

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Questioning your own sources is the practice of treating every cited paper, dataset, model, and claim as a candidate for verification rather than as settled background. In literature review and evidence synthesis, it covers checking whether a source actually supports the sentence it is attached to, whether the source is primary or secondary, and whether the source's method and population fit the question at hand. The site's library of 135 research papers gives a bounded setting for this work, but the same discipline applies to any corpus. It also includes questioning the review's own search strategy, inclusion rules, and citation choices, not only the sources of others.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure for questioning sources is a mix of reference managers, full text access, metadata standards, and version control for notes. A reviewer needs stable identifiers such as DOIs, links to original papers rather than summaries, and a way to record why a source was included or excluded. The site's practice of linking to the original paper rather than to a search tool summary is an example of this infrastructure choice. When a synthesis involves 12,233 extracted claims, the infrastructure must support claim level provenance, not just a bibliography.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method is to read the source, not just the abstract, and to compare the claim in the review against the source's own words, tables, and limitations. A reviewer checks the study design, sample, measures, and analysis, then asks whether the source's conclusion follows from its evidence. For each source, the reviewer records the exact passage or figure that supports the claim, notes any disagreement with other sources, and flags where the source is a preprint, a review, or an opinion piece. This process is repeated across the corpus, with spot checks on sources that are cited most often or that carry the most weight in the synthesis.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance means knowing who produced the source, when, under what funding, and with what corrections or retractions. Rights and risk include copyright limits on text reuse, licensing terms for datasets and models, and the reputational risk of citing a source that has been retracted or misrepresented. A review that links to the original paper, rather than to a search tool summary, gives readers a direct path to check the claim. The reviewer also has a duty to disclose conflicts, to respect embargoes and confidentiality, and to correct the record if a source is later found to be unreliable.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more automated provenance, with claim level extraction, citation context analysis, and tools that flag when a source no longer supports a claim. As language models help draft reviews, the burden shifts from finding sources to verifying them, and the risk of plausible but unsupported citations grows. Expect more emphasis on source audits, reproducibility checks, and open peer review of the evidence trail itself. The aim is not to distrust every source but to make trust earned, specific, and revisable.
